source_text: Quae quoniam, ut locus interim hic patiebatur, munivi, revertamur illo unde digressi sumus; de hoc ipso, ubicumque opportunum fuerit, plenius locuturi. Ecce quanta confessionis luce, et eos qui Baptisma parvulis denegarent, et vos qui eius praeiudicio iustitiam Dei audetis maculare, reprobavi; protestans aliud me non tenere, quam instituta mysteria iisdem, quibus tradita sunt verbis, in omni prorsus aetate esse tractanda, nec pro causarum varietate debere mutari; verum fieri peccatorem ex malo perfecte bonum; innocentem autem, qui nullum habet malum propriae voluntatis, ex bono fieri meliorem, id est, optimum; ut ambo quidem in Christi membra transeant consecrati; sed unus deprehensus in mala vita, alter in bona natura. Ille enim innocentiam, quam exortus acceperat, prava actione corrupit; hic vero sine laude, sine crimine voluntatis, hoc solum habet, quod a Deo conditore suscepit, qui infucata primaevitate felicior, bonum simplicitatis suae vitiare non potuit, nullum habens de actibus meritum, sed hoc solum retinens, quod tanti opificis dignatione possedit.
pass_a_gloss: Which things since, as this place meanwhile was allowing, I have fortified, let us return there from where we have stepped aside; about this itself, wherever it shall have been opportune, about to speak more fully. See with how great a light of confession I have reproved both those who would deny Baptism to little ones, and you who by its prejudgment dare to stain the justice of God; protesting that I hold nothing other than that the instituted mysteries are to be treated in absolutely every age with the same words with which they have been handed down, nor ought they to be changed for variety of cases; but that a sinner becomes from evil perfectly good; but the innocent, who has no evil of his own will, becomes from good better, that is, best; so that both indeed pass consecrated into the members of Christ; but one caught in an evil life, the other in a good nature. For that one corrupted by a crooked action the innocence which he had received at coming-forth; but this one, without praise, without a charge of will, has this only which he took up from God the founder, who, happier by unpainted first-age, could not vitiate the good of his own simplicity, having no desert from acts, but retaining this only which he possessed by the condescension of so great a craftsman.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS parvulus; Blaise infants in original-sin debate

pass_b_english: Having defended these points as far as the present passage allowed, let us return to where we left off. We will discuss this very subject more fully wherever an opportunity arises. See with what a clear confession I rejected both those who would deny baptism to infants and you who dare to stain God's justice by what you claim baptism presupposes. I testified that I hold nothing other than this: the established mysteries must be administered at absolutely every age in the same words in which they were handed down, and must not be changed to suit different cases. But the sinner becomes completely good from being evil, while the innocent person, who has no evil of his own will, becomes better from being good, that is, becomes best. Both are consecrated and pass into Christ's members (compare 1 Corinthians 12:13), but one is found in an evil life and the other in a good nature. The former corrupted by wrongdoing the innocence he received at birth. The latter, without praise or blame attaching to his will, has only what he received from God his Creator. Happier in the unpainted freshness of his earliest age, he has been unable to spoil the goodness of his simplicity. He has earned nothing through deeds but retains only what the kindness of so great a maker gave him.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
